title: Job interviews
desc: A job interview is a conversation to see if you and the role are a good fit. Read the job post, prepare a few examples of work or school you have done, and be ready to ask one or two questions about the job. Arrive a little early, listen carefully, and send a short thank-you message afterward.

what to wear to a job interview

title: Tipping
desc: Tipping is an extra payment for service, common in U.S. restaurants, hair salons and for delivery. Many people tip about 15 to 20 percent of the pre-tax bill for table service when the service was fine. Check the receipt; some places already add a service charge. Rules differ by country, so look it up when you travel.
prompts: what is a normal tip at a restaurant
do i tip if a service charge is already added
do i tip on the tax or the food

title: Opening a bank account
desc: To open a checking or savings account, a bank or credit union usually asks for photo ID, your Social Security number or ITIN if you have one, and a small opening deposit. Compare fees, overdraft rules and whether you need a parent or guardian as a joint owner if you are under 18. Read the account agreement before you sign.
prompts: how do i open a bank account
what do i need to open a checking account
can a teenager open a bank account
bank account id and social security number
do i need a parent to open an account

title: Gross versus net pay
desc: Gross pay is what you earn before deductions. Net pay, or take-home pay, is what you actually receive after taxes and other deductions such as health insurance. Compare job offers by looking at both the pay rate and what is taken out, not only the headline wage.
prompts: why is my paycheck smaller than my wage
gross vs net on a pay stub
why didn't I get the full hourly amount

title: Kitchen knife basics
desc: Keep fingers curled under on the hand that holds the food, and cut with a claw grip so fingertips stay back from the blade. Use a stable board, don't try to catch a falling knife, and wash knives carefully by hand or as the maker directs. A sharp knife is easier to control than a dull one.
prompts: how should i hold a kitchen knife
what is a claw grip when cutting
should i use a sharp or dull knife

title: Boiling versus simmering
desc: Boiling means the liquid is at 212°F (100°C) at sea level, with large, rolling bubbles. Simmering is gentler, with small bubbles that rise slowly, usually just below a boil. Use a boil for pasta or reducing a liquid quickly, and a simmer for soups, sauces and tougher cuts of food that need steady, gentle heat.
prompts: what's the difference between boiling and simmering
when should I simmer instead of boil

title: Sautéing
desc: Sautéing is cooking food quickly in a little oil or butter over medium-high heat, usually in a wide pan. Heat the pan first, don't crowd the food so it browns instead of steaming, and stir or toss as it cooks. Cut pieces to a similar size so they finish at the same time.
prompts: why shouldn't I crowd the pan
heat the pan before the food
cook quickly in a little oil
medium high heat in a skillet

title: Baking versus roasting
desc: Baking and roasting both use dry oven heat. People usually say baking for breads, cakes and other batters, and roasting for meats and vegetables, often at a higher temperature so the outside browns. Follow the recipe temperature and use the rack position it calls for.
prompts: what's the difference between baking and roasting
is roasting the same as baking

title: Scrambling eggs
desc: Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt. Warm a little butter or oil in a nonstick pan over medium-low heat, pour in the eggs, and stir gently as they set. Take them off the heat while they still look slightly moist; they keep cooking in the pan.

title: Boiling eggs
desc: Place eggs in a saucepan and cover them with an inch of cold water. Bring to a boil, then turn off the heat, cover, and let sit: about 6 to 8 minutes for a jammy yolk, or 10 to 12 minutes for a firm hard-boiled yolk. Move the eggs to cold water so they stop cooking and are easier to peel.
prompts: how long to hard boil an egg
why put boiled eggs in cold water
how to make soft boiled eggs
cover eggs with water and boil

title: Food safety temperatures
desc: Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) and ground beef to 160°F (71°C). Steaks and chops are often considered safe at 145°F (63°C) with a short rest, and leftovers should be reheated to 165°F. Use a food thermometer in the thickest part, not just color, and keep cold food at or below 40°F (4°C).
prompts: what temperature should chicken be cooked to
how hot should leftovers be reheated

title: Storing leftovers
desc: Cool leftovers and refrigerate them within two hours, or within one hour if the food has been in a hot room. Use shallow containers so they cool faster, eat or freeze them within a few days, and reheat until steaming hot. When in doubt, throw it out rather than risk leftover food that smells or looks off.
prompts: how long can leftovers stay in the fridge
should I throw out old leftovers

title: Defrosting food safely
desc: The safest ways to thaw food are in the refrigerator, under cold running water, or in the microwave if you will cook it right away. Do not thaw meat or poultry on the counter at room temperature, where the outside can sit in the danger zone while the inside is still frozen. Cook food thawed in the microwave immediately.
prompts: how do i defrost meat safely
can I thaw chicken on the counter
is it safe to defrost in the microwave
don't leave meat out to thaw

title: Preventing cross-contamination
desc: Cross-contamination is when germs from raw meat, poultry or seafood get onto ready-to-eat food. Use separate cutting boards or wash the board, knife and hands with hot soapy water after cutting raw meat. Keep raw meat on a plate on the bottom fridge shelf so juices cannot drip onto other food.
prompts: should I use a separate cutting board for meat
raw chicken on the same board as salad
how to avoid spreading germs in the kitchen
raw meat on the bottom shelf
keeping ready to eat food safe

title: Best-by and use-by dates
desc: A use-by or expiration date is about safety for some foods, especially infant formula, and you should follow it. A best-by or best-before date is usually about quality, not an automatic deadline; many foods are still fine if they were stored well and show no spoilage. When a food looks, smells or feels wrong, do not eat it even if the date has not passed.
prompts: what's the difference between best by and use by
is it safe to eat food after the best by date
does best by mean it is spoiled
food looks fine but date passed

title: Making oatmeal
desc: For stovetop oats, use about 2 cups of water or milk per 1 cup of rolled oats, a pinch of salt, and simmer, stirring, until thick and creamy, often 5 minutes. Quick oats cook faster; steel-cut oats take longer and need more liquid. Sweeten or add fruit after cooking if you want.
prompts: how long do oats take to cook

title: Making pancakes
desc: Mix the dry ingredients, then the wet, and stir just until combined; a few lumps are fine and help keep pancakes tender. Cook on a greased medium pan until bubbles form and the edges look set, then flip once and cook the other side. Keep the heat moderate so the inside cooks before the outside burns.
prompts: when do I flip a pancake

title: Making a grilled cheese
desc: Butter the outside of two bread slices, add cheese between them, and cook in a skillet over medium-low heat until the bread is golden and the cheese has melted, flipping once. Covering the pan for a minute can help the cheese melt without burning the bread.

title: Making a quesadilla
desc: Scatter cheese and any fillings on one half of a tortilla, fold it over, and cook in a lightly oiled skillet over medium heat until both sides are golden and the cheese melts. Let it sit a minute before cutting so the filling doesn't slide out.

title: Salting pasta water
desc: Salt the water after it is boiling, just before you add the pasta. The pasta absorbs some of that seasoning as it cooks, so the finished dish tastes better than if you only salt the sauce. A common starting point is about 1 tablespoon of kosher salt per 4 quarts of water, then adjust to your taste and any doctor's advice on sodium.
prompts: when do I add salt to pasta water
why salt the water for pasta
how much salt in pasta water

title: Microwave safety
desc: Use microwave-safe glass or labeled plastic, not metal or foil, which can spark. Watch out for steam when you uncover a hot container, and stir food so it heats evenly. Superheated water can erupt, so use a microwave-safe container and care when heating plain water. If a dish says do not microwave, follow that.

steam burn from a microwave lid
can foil go in the microwave

title: Grease fires
desc: If oil in a pan catches fire, turn off the heat if you can do it safely and slide a metal lid over the pan to smother the flames. Never pour water on a grease fire; it can explode the fire outward. Baking soda can help on a small pan fire. If the fire is spreading, leave, close the door, and call 911.

title: American football downs
desc: A down is one play. The offense has four downs to gain 10 yards. If they succeed, they get a new set of downs. If they don't, the other team usually takes over. Teams often punt or try a field goal on fourth down instead of risking a turnover on downs.

title: Touchdowns and field goals
desc: A touchdown is worth 6 points when the ball is carried or caught in the opponent's end zone. The team can then try an extra point kick (1) or a two-point conversion. A field goal is normally 3 points, kicked through the goalposts, often on fourth down or at the end of a half.

how do you score in football

title: Baseball strikes and innings
desc: A strike is a pitch in the strike zone that the batter does not hit fairly, or a swing and a miss, or a foul (except a foul cannot be strike three unless it is a bunt). Three strikes make an out. An inning is a turn for both teams to bat; a regulation game is usually nine innings.

how long is a baseball game

title: Golf scoring
desc: In stroke play, the person with the fewest total shots wins. Par is the expected number of strokes for a hole. A birdie is one under par, an eagle is two under, and a bogey is one over par. Lower totals are better.

title: Freestyle swimming
desc: Freestyle usually means the front crawl: alternate arm strokes, a flutter kick, and breathing to the side. Keep your body fairly long and level, and turn your head to breathe rather than lifting it straight up. In a freestyle event you may use any stroke, but crawl is the fastest for most people.

title: Basketball layups
desc: A layup is a close-range shot off the backboard while moving toward the hoop. Dribble in, pick up the ball, and jump off the opposite foot from the shooting hand: right-hand layup, jump off the left foot. Use the backboard square as a target, and protect the ball with your body.

title: Chess check and checkmate
desc: Check means your king is under attack and you must get out of it by moving the king, blocking the attack, or capturing the attacking piece. Checkmate means the king is in check and there is no legal way out, so the game is over and that player loses. You cannot make a move that leaves your own king in check.

title: Castling
desc: Castling is a special king-and-rook move: the king moves two squares toward a rook, and that rook jumps to the square the king crossed. You can castle only if neither piece has moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check and does not pass through or land on an attacked square.

title: Sudoku
desc: Sudoku is a puzzle on a 9-by-9 grid divided into 3-by-3 boxes. Fill every row, column and box with the digits 1 through 9, each used once. Start with cells that have the fewest possibilities, pencil in candidates, and never guess if a logical next number is available.
prompts: 1 to 9 in each row column and box

title: Uno
desc: In Uno, you take turns playing a card that matches the color or number (or symbol) of the card on the pile, or you play a wild. Draw if you cannot play. Action cards can skip, reverse, or make the next player draw. Say “Uno” when you have one card left, or you may have to draw if someone catches you.

title: In-game purchases
desc: In-game purchases are optional items, currency or passes you buy with real money inside a game. Set a password, use purchase approvals, and check platform spending limits so a game cannot charge you by accident. Treat leftover currency as money already spent, and don't feel you have to buy an advantage to play.

title: Checking tire pressure
desc: Look up the recommended PSI on the driver's door sticker, not only the tire sidewall, which shows the maximum. Check when the tires are cold, unscrew the valve cap, press a gauge on the valve, and add or release air until you hit the number. Recheck all four tires, and the spare if you have one.

title: Pumping gas
desc: Park at the pump, turn the car off, and open the fuel door. Choose the grade your owner's manual recommends, usually regular unless the car requires premium. Insert the nozzle fully, pump, then wait a moment, hang the nozzle up, and tighten the cap until it clicks if it is a click cap. Don't smoke or use your phone in a way that distracts you at the pump.

title: Checking engine oil
desc: Park on level ground, turn the engine off, and wait a few minutes. Pull out the dipstick, wipe it, put it back in fully, then pull it out again and read the level between the min and max marks. If it is low, add the oil type in your owner's manual a little at a time and recheck. A warning light or a very low level means you should not keep driving.

title: Jump-starting a car
desc: Only jump-start if both batteries are the same voltage, usually 12 volts, and you know the correct terminals. Connect the red clamp to the dead battery's positive terminal, then to the good battery's positive. Connect the black clamp to the good battery's negative, then to an unpainted metal ground on the dead car, not the dead negative terminal if the manual says not to. Start the good car, then the dead one, and remove the cables in reverse order. If you are unsure, call for roadside help.

title: Changing a spare tire
desc: Pull well off the road, turn on hazard lights, and set the parking brake. Loosen the lug nuts slightly before jacking, jack at the lift point in the owner's manual, remove the nuts, swap the wheel, snug the nuts, lower the car, then tighten the nuts in a star pattern. A donut spare is usually for short, slower trips to a shop, not highway speeds for long distances.

title: Dashboard warning lights
desc: A red oil, brake or temperature warning usually means you should stop safely as soon as you can and check the manual or get help. An amber check-engine or tire light often means something needs service soon, but not always an instant stop. Look up the exact symbol in your owner's manual instead of ignoring a light.

title: Seat belts
desc: A seat belt should sit across the hips and mid-chest, not the stomach or neck, and it should be snug. Everyone in the car should buckle up, including the back seat. A belt works with the airbag; sitting too close or leaving the belt off can make a crash much more dangerous.

title: Car insurance basics
desc: Car insurance helps pay for damage or injury after a crash, theft or other covered events, according to your policy. Liability coverage pays others if you are at fault; collision and comprehensive cover damage to your own car in different situations. State laws set minimums, and a deductible is what you pay first before the insurer pays the rest.

title: Getting a learner's permit
desc: A learner's permit lets you practice driving with restrictions before a full license. Rules vary by state, but you usually have to be a minimum age, pass a written knowledge test and an eye test, and complete an application with ID and, if you are a minor, a parent or guardian's consent. Drive only with the passengers and hours your state allows.

title: Parallel parking
desc: Line up with the car in front of the space, about two to three feet away. Reverse and turn toward the curb to enter the space, then straighten and turn the other way to tuck the bumper in. You should end up a reasonable distance from the curb, usually within about 12 inches in many tests, without hitting the cars around you. Practice in an empty lot first.

turn toward the curb then straighten

title: Pedestrian safety
desc: Cross at a corner or marked crosswalk when you can, look left, right, then left again, and make sure drivers have stopped before you step out. On a two-way street, watch for turning cars. At night, wear something visible, and stay off your phone while crossing. Drivers should yield, but do not assume they have seen you.

title: Locking a bicycle
desc: Lock the frame and if you can a wheel to a solid rack, using a sturdy U-lock or a quality heavy chain, not only a thin cable. Don't leave the lock near the ground where it is easier to attack, and take lights and loose bags with you. Register the bike and photograph the serial number in case it is stolen.

title: Tying a necktie
desc: For a common four-in-hand knot, drape the tie around your neck with the wide end hanging lower. Wrap the wide end across the narrow end, around the back, and across the front again, then up through the neck loop and down through the front knot. Slide the knot up and dimple the center if you want a neater look.

title: Sewing on a button
desc: Thread a needle and knot the end. From the back of the fabric, sew through each pair of buttonholes several times, leaving a tiny shank of thread under the button if the fabric is thick, then wrap the thread around that shank and knot it on the back. Match the thread color and don't pull so tight that the fabric puckers.

title: Using a fire extinguisher
desc: Use a fire extinguisher only if the fire is small, you have a clear exit, and you know what is burning. Remember PASS: pull the pin, aim at the base of the fire, squeeze the handle, and sweep from side to side. If the fire grows or the room fills with smoke, leave and call 911.

title: Smoke alarms
desc: Smoke alarms should be on every level of a home, inside bedrooms, and outside sleeping areas. Test them monthly, replace batteries when the unit chirps or as the maker directs, and replace the whole alarm when it reaches the date on the back, often after about 10 years. Never take the battery out just to stop a nuisance chirp without fixing the cause.

title: Airport security basics
desc: At U.S. airport security, have your ID and boarding pass ready, and follow the bin rules for shoes, laptops and liquids. Liquids in carry-on bags generally must be in containers of 3.4 ounces (100 ml) or less, in one quart-size bag, with exceptions such as medically necessary items you should declare. Put metal items in a bin, and wait for the officer's instructions.
